verdictSummary: zcal's solo core is compact: build a personal freeform scheduling tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back. A competent builder can reach a useful personal version in one sitting, while the paid product mainly wins on OAuth, calendar reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Build a personal freeform scheduling tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
replacementScope: personal replacement for the core loop
whatYouLose: reliable reminders and timezone edge cases
calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness
whyPeopleStillPay: zcal: People pay because a booking tool must never double-book them, leak private events, or send the wrong time to a client.
ongoingBurden: Maintain OAuth, timezone data, webhooks, idempotency, reminders, calendar-provider quirks, and uptime.

priorArt.name: Cal.com
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source scheduling platform and OAuth reference.

alternatives.name: Calendly Free
alternatives.desc: One active event type and unlimited bookings; meeting polls survive, workflows and teams do not.

facts.install: Hosted signup and one calendar connection
facts.dataFormat: Event-type settings, invitee answers, scheduling activity and account data live in Calendly's cloud; confirmed meetings are synchronized to the connected calendar, and the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: Calendly Free is dependable for one active event type, but zcal's personalized pages and group-poll experience become harder to reproduce once more than one booking flow is needed.
facts.setupBlocker: Setup is clean, but the permanent free account is limited to one one-to-one event type and one connected calendar.

alternatives.name: TidyCal Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited one-person booking types and paid bookings on one calendar; group meetings and fancy emails cost extra.

facts.install: Hosted signup and one calendar connection
facts.dataFormat: Booking types, attendee answers and booking records live in TidyCal's cloud and are synchronized to the connected calendar; the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: TidyCal Free handles one-person booking links, but one connected calendar and no free group-meeting workflow make it a poor substitute for zcal's polls and multi-person scheduling.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no technical install hurdle, but free accounts get only one calendar connection and omit automatic video links, group meetings, custom emails, exports, analytics and API access.

alternatives.name: YouCanBookMe Free
alternatives.desc: One booking page, but it keeps forms, payments, confirmations, polls and the calendar-overlay trick.

facts.install: Hosted signup and one calendar connection
facts.dataFormat: Booking-page configuration, form answers and appointment records live in YouCanBookMe's cloud, with events synchronized to the connected calendar; the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: YouCanBookMe Free retains capable booking forms and polls, but one booking page and one connected calendar sharply limit the personalized set of scheduling pages zcal is built around.
facts.setupBlocker: The setup itself is clean; the first hard limit is one booking page and one connected calendar.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Rallly
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A superb poller, but it does not also provide reusable one-to-one scheduling links.

notes: Strong page because zcal separates a compact personal workflow from the value of long-term polish.
prompt:
Build a usable personal replacement for the core loop of zcal.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a personal freeform scheduling tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: multi-calendar conflict handling; race-free booking under load; team routing and round robin.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
